876.title: Umar's death
876.hook: stabbed at dawn prayer, he names a council of six to choose his successor
876.howItsDone: Muslims retell Umar's death from the long report in Sahih al-Bukhari, and the council he named is taught in Sunni history as the shura that chose Uthman; his grave lies beside the Prophet's and Abu Bakr's in Medina.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plague, and a caravan that turned back from God's decree to God's decree. Your line was: don't enter, don't leave. What step did you take for your health? Day eight hundred seventy-six.

Dawn in the mosque at Medina. The rows are forming. Umar walks between them as he used to before the prayer, telling people to straighten their lines. He takes his place at the front and says God is greatest. And in that moment a man steps out of the dark and stabs him. A man named Amr ibn Maymun was standing in the rows, and Bukhari keeps what he saw. Today: Umar's death.
screen: `DAWN, AND THE ROWS FORMING.` → `GOD IS GREATEST.` → `A MAN STEPS OUT OF THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Umar falls, and the first thing he does is reach for Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf's hand and pull him forward to lead the prayer. The prayer goes on, short and quiet. Afterward Umar asks who struck him. A slave of al-Mughirah, he's told. And Umar says: praise be to God, who did not let my death come at the hands of a man who claims Islam. They bring him milk to drink, and it comes out of the wound, and the people around him understand. A young man comes in and praises him: your companionship with the Prophet, your justice. Umar answers: I wish it would come out even, nothing against me and nothing for me. Then he sends his son Abdullah to Aisha, with a request: may Umar be buried beside his two companions? She says she had wanted the place for herself, but she will give it to him. And then the question everyone is waiting for. Who leads next? Umar does not name a son. He does not name one man. He names six, the companions with whom, he says, the Prophet was pleased when he died: Ali, Uthman, al-Zubayr, Talhah, Sa'd and Abd al-Rahman. Let them choose one from among themselves. His own son may sit with them, but have no share in the choice. The Qur'an praises those whose affairs are settled by consultation among them. Umar made his last act a consultation. Sunni Muslims honor this council as the way Uthman was chosen; Shia Muslims, as with the succession, read these events differently. The council itself is tomorrow's story.
screen: `HE PULLS ABD AL-RAHMAN FORWARD.` · `NOT BY ONE WHO CLAIMS ISLAM.` · `BURIED BESIDE HIS TWO COMPANIONS.` · `SIX NAMED. NO SON, NO HEIR.` · then, large: `A COUNCIL, NOT A CROWN.`

segments.voice: The practice: the dawn prayer. If you pray, you might set an alarm and pray fajr tomorrow, at the hour Umar was standing in the rows. If you don't, you might simply wake a little early tomorrow and sit for a minute at first light. For now, close your eyes if you like. Picture the mosque before sunrise, the rows straight, the quiet. Breathe in, and think of a man who, wounded, made sure the prayer continued. Breathe out. Decide on your dawn. The bell holds the time.
Umar's death. Stabbed as he began the dawn prayer, he had the prayer go on, asked to be buried beside his two companions, and named six to choose from among themselves. Today's word.
Your line: a council, not a crown. Today, before you decide something that affects others, ask them first. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

877.title: Uthman's caliphate
877.hook: the gentle Uthman rules as lands and a navy grow
877.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims honor Uthman as the third rightly guided caliph and remember his modesty and generosity; Shia Muslims hold that Ali was the rightful leader, and Shia tellings dwell on the complaints against Uthman's rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umar's death: struck at the dawn prayer, he left the choice to a council. Your line was a council, not a crown. Did you ask others before deciding something that touched them? Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

Should I not feel shy before a man the angels feel shy before? Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asking that about one of his companions. The scene around it is small. The Prophet is resting at home, his clothes loosely arranged. Abu Bakr comes in, and he stays as he is. Umar comes in, and he stays as he is. Then Uthman asks to enter, and the Prophet sits up and straightens his garment. Aisha asks him why. His answer is that question. The man is Uthman ibn Affan, and after Umar's death the council chose him. Today, the shape of his rule.
screen: `THE PROPHET SITS UP.` → `THE ANGELS FEEL SHY.` → `THE COUNCIL CHOOSES UTHMAN.`

segments.voice: Bukhari records how the choice was made. The men Umar named narrowed it among themselves, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, giving up his own claim, was trusted to choose between Ali and Uthman. He spent nights consulting people, the report says, and in the end he took Uthman's hand and pledged to him, and the people followed. So Uthman began with a reputation already set. In Bukhari's reports he is the one who answered the Prophet's call to provide the well of Rumah for the people, and to equip the army in a time of hardship. Wealthy, quiet, generous, modest. Under his rule the lands of the Muslims kept growing. And something new happened: ships. Bukhari tells of a woman, Umm Haram, who once heard the Prophet describe people of his community riding the sea like kings on thrones. She asked him to pray that she would be one of them. The report says she later sailed, in the days of Mu'awiyah, who served Uthman as governor of Syria, and the histories set that voyage in Uthman's time. Now the harder part. Gentleness in a ruler can be read two ways. His admirers see mercy: a caliph slow to punish, open-handed with his own money. His critics, in his own lifetime, said he gave too many posts to his relatives and was too slow to remove governors people complained about. The sources record both. Sunni Muslims honor him as the third of the rightly guided caliphs and one of the companions promised paradise. Shia Muslims hold that Ali should have led from the start, and Shia tellings dwell on the complaints against Uthman's rule. Both readings are kept here, side by side, with no winner picked, because the complaints will grow, and the next few days will show where they led.
screen: `ABD AL-RAHMAN CONSULTS FOR NIGHTS.` · `A WELL PROVIDED, AN ARMY EQUIPPED.` · `UMM HARAM AND THE SEA.` · `MERCY, OR TOO SOFT?` · then, large: `GENTLE RULE.`

segments.voice: The practice: be gentle in authority. Settle, and breathe. Small kingdoms are everywhere. A kitchen. A classroom. A shift you run. A dog, even. Pick one place where people, or creatures, depend on your decisions. Breathe in, and remember a recent moment there when you were sharper than you needed to be. Breathe out, and picture doing it again, the same decision, but gentler in tone. Same firmness, softer voice. If you pray, you can ask for mercy in how you lead. The bell holds the time.
Uthman's caliphate. The rule of Uthman ibn Affan, chosen by the council after Umar: a modest, generous man, a time of growth and ships at sea, and complaints that would not go away. Today's word.
Your line: gentle rule. Today, give one instruction, to anyone, more gently than you normally would, and see if it still gets done. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

878.title: One reading for all
878.hook: Uthman sends standard copies of the Qur'an to the cities to unite the reading
878.howItsDone: Muslims call a written copy of the Qur'an a mushaf and commonly keep it in a clean, raised place; printed copies today follow the written text remembered as Uthman's, and recognized recitations are still taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uthman's caliphate: a modest man, a growing realm, ships at sea, and complaints beginning. Your line was gentle rule. Did a gentler tone still get the thing done? Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

A soldier comes home from the far frontier, and what is troubling him is not the enemy. It is his own side. The man is Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, and Bukhari tells us what he saw on campaign in the north. Muslims from Syria and Muslims from Iraq were serving together, and when they recited the Qur'an, they recited it differently, and they argued about it. Hudhayfah rides to Medina and goes straight to Uthman. Commander of the faithful, he says, in effect, save this community before it divides over its own book. Today, what Uthman did.
screen: `A SOLDIER COMES HOME WORRIED.` → `TWO ARMIES, TWO READINGS.` → `SAVE THE COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: Bukhari's report is short and practical. Uthman sends to Hafsah, the Prophet's widow and Umar's daughter, who is keeping the sheets of the Qur'an gathered in Abu Bakr's time. He asks to borrow them. Then he gives the work to Zayd ibn Thabit, who had written revelation for the Prophet, together with men of Quraysh, and tells them: where you differ with Zayd over how a word is written, write it in the speech of Quraysh, because the Qur'an came down in their tongue. They copy the sheets into books. Uthman returns the sheets to Hafsah. And he sends a copy out to each province, with an order that other written collections be burned. That last line may startle a modern listener. Burning pages of the Qur'an? The tradition reads it as the opposite of disrespect: one agreed text, so that no one would fight over private copies with their own additions and gaps. Reports say Ali, asked about it later, defended what Uthman did with the copies. Muslims call a written copy a mushaf, and the standard copies are remembered as Uthman's. The Qur'an itself says something about who keeps it. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder, and lo! We verily are its Guardian." Tradition reads Uthman's work as one of the ways that promise was carried out by human hands. And the different ways of reciting were not erased; recognized recitations, the qira'at, are still learned and recited. Unity of the written text, not one single voice.
screen: `HAFSAH LENDS THE SHEETS.` · `ZAYD COPIES IN THE SPEECH OF QURAYSH.` · `A COPY TO EACH PROVINCE.` · `THE REMINDER AND ITS GUARDIAN.` · then, large: `ONE TEXT FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: The practice: treat your copy with care. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Qur'an nearby, look at where it sits. Is it on a high shelf, on the floor, under a coffee cup? If you don't have one, choose any book that matters to you, a scripture, a family Bible, a grandparent's letters. Breathe in, and notice its weight, its wear, the hands it has passed through. Breathe out. If you can, move it to a cleaner, higher place, or wrap it, or simply wipe the cover. One small act of care for the page. The bell holds the time.
Mushaf, a written copy of the Qur'an: Uthman's standard copies, made from Hafsah's sheets and sent to the provinces, so the community would share one written text. Today's word.

Your line: one text for all. Today, in a disagreement, try going back to the shared page, the agreed plan, the actual words, before arguing about whose memory is right. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

879.title: The siege
879.hook: grievances grow, rebels surround his house, and he refuses to let blood be shed for him
879.howItsDone: The histories name the siege of Uthman as the start of the fitnah; Sunni teachers cite his refusal to let Muslims fight on his behalf, and Shia tellings put the weight on the grievances behind the revolt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mushaf: Hafsah's sheets, Zayd's copies, a mushaf for each province. Your line was one text for all. Did going back to the shared page settle anything? Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

The street outside the caliph's house is full of armed men, and they are not foreign soldiers. They are Muslims, come from Egypt and from the garrison towns of Iraq with complaints about governors, about appointments, about money. They have camped in Medina. They want Uthman to step down. He will not take off what God has put on him, he says. So they close in on his house. Inside are a few companions and young men, among them, the histories say, Hasan, the Prophet's grandson, sent by Ali to guard the door. They have swords. They are ready. And the old man inside tells them to put the swords away. Today's word names what had begun.
screen: `ARMED MEN IN THE STREET.` → `STEP DOWN, THEY SAY.` → `PUT THE SWORDS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Fitnah. In the Qur'an the word carries the sense of trial, temptation and testing, and the lexicons connect the root with the smelting of gold in fire to see what is real. Later Muslims also use it for civil strife, Muslim against Muslim, because that is a test of a different kind. The histories give the name to the years that begin at Uthman's door. Why did he refuse a defense? The sources point back to the Prophet. Bukhari records a day when the Prophet sat at a well and the companions came one by one asking to enter. For Abu Bakr he said, give him the good news of paradise. For Umar the same. For Uthman, the good news of paradise, with a trial that will befall him. Uthman heard it, the report says, and answered: God is the one whose help is sought. And Tirmidhi records the Prophet telling Uthman that God might clothe him in a shirt, and if people wanted him to take it off, he should not. Uthman read these as a calling: keep the office, and do not let Muslims kill Muslims to save his life. So, the histories report, he told those guarding him to go home. He told the servants who would fight that whoever laid down his weapon was free. Readers have argued about this ever since. Was it holiness, or did it hand the city to the rebels? Sunni tradition honors it as the restraint of a martyr. Shia tellings put the weight instead on the grievances he had not answered. The sources agree on the core: he forbade fighting for him.
screen: `FITNAH: TRIAL BY FIRE.` · `PARADISE, WITH A TRIAL.` · `DO NOT TAKE OFF THE SHIRT.` · `GO HOME. LAY DOWN YOUR WEAPON.` · then, large: `HE FORBADE FIGHTING FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: refuse to escalate. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one conflict that is live right now: a family thread, a neighbor, a coworker, a comment section. Find the move you've been tempted to make, the reply that would bring in your allies, the screenshot you'd send to win. Breathe in, and hold that move in your hand. Breathe out, and set it down. Not giving up what's right, just declining to raise the stakes today. If you pray, you can ask for help in the trial. The bell holds the time.
Fitnah. Trial and testing in the Qur'an, and later the name for strife among Muslims, beginning, the histories say, with the siege of Uthman's house. Today's word.
Your line: he forbade fighting for him. Today, when someone offers to take your side in a quarrel, thank them, and ask them to stay out of it. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

880.title: Uthman killed
880.hook: Uthman is killed in his house, reading the Qur'an
880.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims remember Uthman as a martyr killed while reading the Qur'an and often pray for mercy on him when his name is mentioned; Shia Muslims remember the event as part of the history that led to Ali's caliphate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the siege, and the word fitnah: a trial that tests what is real. Your line was he forbade fighting for him. Did you keep someone out of a quarrel that was yours? Day eight hundred eighty.

On the mountain of Uhud, years earlier, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stood with three companions: Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman. Bukhari reports that the mountain trembled beneath them, and the Prophet said to it, be still, Uhud, for on you are a prophet, a man of truth, and two martyrs. Umar had already died that way, struck at prayer. Now the second martyr in that saying comes due. Uthman's friends have put their swords away, as he asked. The swords outside have not been put away. Today, his last day.
screen: `THE MOUNTAIN TREMBLES.` → `A PROPHET, A MAN OF TRUTH, TWO MARTYRS.` → `THE SECOND MARTYR COMES DUE.`

segments.voice: The histories tell it plainly, and with some differences in detail. The defenders have gone home, as he asked. Uthman is in his room with a copy of the Qur'an open in front of him, reading. Some reports say he was fasting that day, and had seen the Prophet in a dream the night before, telling him he would break his fast with him. The attackers come in, some say over the wall from a neighboring house. His wife, Na'ilah, throws herself between him and the blade, and her hand is cut. Uthman is struck while the book is still open. Tradition says his blood fell on a verse from the second surah, a line in which God promises to be enough against those who oppose. Whether or not every detail is exact, the picture the tradition keeps is the one in your line: an old man, unarmed, killed with the book open. For Sunni Muslims, he is a martyr, the man of whom the Prophet said the angels feel shy, and a companion promised paradise. Shia Muslims, who hold that leadership belonged to Ali, do not honor his rule in the same way, and their historians emphasize the grievances that came before. Across those differences, the histories tell it as a catastrophe. A caliph of the Muslims was killed by Muslims in the city of the Prophet. The fitnah was no longer a threat. It had arrived, and the question of who would lead next would split the community for years to come.
screen: `READING, WITH THE BOOK OPEN.` · `NA'ILAH STEPS BETWEEN.` · `A VERSE STAINED, TRADITION SAYS.` · `A CALIPH KILLED IN MEDINA.` · then, large: `KILLED WITH THE BOOK OPEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: read a page in his memory. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Qur'an, open it anywhere, or to the second surah, and read one page slowly, in Arabic or in translation, whatever you can. If you don't have one, read any page of a book that matters to you, and read it as if someone would give their life to keep it open. Don't rush toward the end of the page. Let each line land. If you pray, you can ask mercy for the dead. The bell holds the time.
Uthman killed. The third caliph, for Sunni Muslims, killed in his house in Medina by Muslim rebels, reading the Qur'an, after forbidding anyone to fight for him. Today's word.
Your line: killed with the book open. Today, keep one page open longer than usual, a scripture, a letter, a hard email, and read it to the end before you answer. Day eight hundred eighty.

881.title: Ali, caliph
881.hook: Ali accepts the caliphate in a divided city, the fourth caliph for Sunnis, the first Imam for Shia
881.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims honor Ali as the fourth rightly guided caliph; Shia Muslims honor him as the first Imam, appointed by the Prophet, and both remember the hadith of Aaron and Moses about him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uthman killed: in his own house, unarmed, killed with the book open. Did you read one page to the end before answering? Today a new part begins, the years of Ali. Day eight hundred eighty-one.

Who wants a crown the day after the last man wearing it was murdered? Medina is in shock. The caliph's blood is barely dry, the rebels are still in the streets, and the city needs someone to lead it, today. The people go to one man's door: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin, raised in his house, married to his daughter Fatimah. And the reports say his first answer was no. Leave me, he tells them, find someone else; I would rather be your helper than your ruler. They keep coming back. Today's word is his name.
screen: `A CITY IN SHOCK.` → `THEY GO TO ALI'S DOOR.` → `LEAVE ME, HE SAYS.`

segments.voice: In the end, the histories say, Ali agreed, on one condition: the pledge would not be made in private, but openly, in the mosque, where everyone could see. So he became caliph in a divided city, and some companions held back from pledging at all. Now here is where Muslims tell the same story in two ways, and both deserve to be heard plainly. For Sunni Muslims, Ali is the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs, after Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman, each one chosen in turn, and all four honored. For Shia Muslims, Ali is the first Imam, the one the Prophet named to lead after him, and the three before him held an office that was rightfully his. That is your line: the fourth; the first. Same man, same day, two counts. Both traditions keep one saying about him, and Shia collections carry it too. In Bukhari's telling, that when the Prophet left Ali behind in Medina during a campaign, Ali was unhappy, and the Prophet said to him: are you not content to be to me as Aaron was to Moses, except that there will be no prophet after me? And the saying from Ghadir Khumm, met earlier in this part, comes back now with new weight: of whomever I am the mawla, Ali is his mawla. A word of love and loyalty, in the Sunni reading; an appointment to lead, in the Shia reading. Either way, the man who took up the office that day was not taking a prize. He was taking on a fitnah already burning, and a community that would not agree on how to count him.
screen: `THE PLEDGE MADE OPENLY.` · `SUNNI: THE FOURTH CALIPH.` · `SHIA: THE FIRST IMAM.` · `AS AARON WAS TO MOSES.` · then, large: `THE FOURTH; THE FIRST.`

segments.voice: The practice: take up a hard duty. Settle, and breathe. Maybe there is one thing left at the door, hoping someone else will pick it up. The difficult conversation. The care of an aging parent this week. The project nobody wants. Breathe in, and look at it honestly. You don't have to finish it. Breathe out, and decide on one first step you will take, openly, where it can be seen and counted on. If you pray, you can ask for strength for the duty. The bell holds the time.
Ali. Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law: the fourth rightly guided caliph for Sunni Muslims, and the first Imam for Shia Muslims. Today's word.
Your line: the fourth; the first. Today, when you hear a story told two ways, say both out loud before you choose a side, if you choose at all. Day eight hundred eighty-one.

882.title: The Battle of the Camel
882.hook: Aisha, Talhah and Zubayr oppose Ali, and believers fight believers
882.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims teach the Battle of the Camel as a tragedy among honored companions who acted on their judgment; Shia Muslims teach it as Ali's rightful defense of his caliphate. Both recite the verse on making peace between two parties of believers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ali: reluctant, pledged openly in the mosque. Your line was the fourth; the first. Did you hear a story told two ways and say both? Day eight hundred eighty-two.

A camel stands in the middle of a battlefield outside Basra. On its back is a covered litter, and inside the litter is Aisha, the Prophet's widow, the woman Muslims call a mother of the believers. Around the camel, men are dying to protect it. Facing them is the army of Ali, the Prophet's cousin. With Aisha are Talhah and Zubayr, two companions the Prophet had promised paradise. Every name on this field belongs to the Prophet's own circle. That is what makes the day so hard to tell. Today, the battle named after an animal.
screen: `A CAMEL ON THE FIELD.` → `AISHA IN THE LITTER.` → `THE PROPHET'S OWN CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: How did it come to this? Uthman's killers were still among the crowds. Aisha, Talhah and Zubayr demanded that justice for his blood come first. Ali held that the state had to be steadied before the guilty could be found and punished. Both sides said they wanted justice for Uthman. They disagreed about the order. Aisha's party went to Basra. Ali followed. The histories say talks went far, and a settlement seemed close, and then fighting broke out, some reports say in the night, stirred up by men who feared any peace would expose them. Bukhari keeps a moment from just before. Ammar ibn Yasir, on Ali's side, stands in the pulpit at Kufa and says of Aisha: she is the wife of your Prophet in this world and the next, but God is testing you, whether you will obey Him or her. Even from the other side, Ammar would not speak of her without honor. The Qur'an had already named this kind of day. In Pickthall's translation: "And if two parties of believers fall to fighting, then make peace between them." Two parties of believers. The verse does not say one side stops being believers. Ali's army won. Talhah and Zubayr were killed. The histories say Ali then sent Aisha back to Medina with honor and an escort. Sunni teaching holds that the companions on both sides were acting on their best judgment, and honors them all. Shia Muslims hold that Ali was in the right and that those who fought him erred. Your line holds what both sides grieve: believers against believers.
screen: `JUSTICE FIRST, OR ORDER FIRST?` · `PEACE CLOSE, THEN FIGHTING.` · `TWO PARTIES OF BELIEVERS.` · `AISHA SENT HOME WITH HONOR.` · then, large: `BELIEVERS AGAINST BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray, or hope, for peace between Muslims. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place where Muslims are divided right now, a country, a city, a mosque committee, a family. You don't need to know who is right. Breathe in, and hold both sides in mind at once, honored people on each. Breathe out. If you pray, you can ask God, in your own words, to make peace between them, as the verse asks of believers. If you don't, simply wish them peace. The bell holds the time.
The Battle of the Camel. The fight at Basra between Ali's army and the party of Aisha, Talhah and Zubayr, named for the camel that carried Aisha's litter. Today's word.
screen: `THE BATTLE OF THE CAMEL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: believers against believers. Today, if you're in a quarrel with someone you respect, say one honoring thing about them, to them or about them, while you still disagree. Day eight hundred eighty-two.
